records.value: (a) The top number is the horizontal movement (positive means east, negative means west). The bottom number is the vertical movement (positive means north, negative means south). (b) |w| = √((−6)² + 5²) = √(36 + 25) = √61 ≈ 7.8 km. |s| = √(5² + (−6)²) = √(25 + 36) = √61 ≈ 7.8 km. (c) The two magnitudes are equal to each other and close to the 8 km on the map but not exactly 8 km, because the grid coordinates are approximate readings from a simplified map. The point is that both journeys have a size of about 8 km, so the scalar distance alone cannot tell them apart. (d) The magnitude is a scalar, so it keeps only the size and discards the direction. Each component of w has the opposite sign to the matching component of s, so they point in roughly opposite directions (they are not exactly opposite, because the vectors are not parallel) and are not equivalent vectors. Their endpoints are therefore far apart, which is why the matatus arrive at different destinations. With east and north positive, w points north-west towards Westlands and s points south-east towards South B, matching the map.
records.why: Knock-on: exemplar recomputed for s = (5; −6): √(25+36) = √61 ≈ 7.8 km, equal to |w|. It also states that the vectors are roughly, not exactly, opposite.

records.value: Time budget for the 40-minute period: Predict 6, Observe 9, Explain 13, Driving Question Board 5, Model Building 6, transitions 1. Lesson 1 opens the entire Vectors unit by presenting the anchoring phenomenon: a simplified Nairobi street grid map showing two matatu routes from Kencom Bus Stop, both labelled 8 km, yet ending at Westlands (northwest) and South B (southeast) respectively. This visible contradiction between equal distances and completely different destinations drives a whole-class prediction activity, surfaces prior knowledge of distance and direction, and creates an authentic need for the concept of a vector. The teacher then introduces the terms 'vector' and 'scalar' with Kenyan-context examples, and learners classify a set of everyday quantities. The lesson closes by opening the class Driving Question Board (DQB) where learners post their burning questions for the unit. No computation is required in this lesson; the focus is entirely on conceptual anchoring, vocabulary introduction, and curiosity generation.

records.value: SETUP (before class): Project or print the simplified Nairobi street grid map. Mark Kencom Bus Stop clearly at the centre. Draw Route A (northwest arrow, labelled '8 km → Westlands') and Route B (southeast arrow, labelled '8 km → South B'). Include one-way road signs and directional arrows on a few roads to prime direction thinking. LAUNCH AND SILENT MAP READING (1 min): Point to the map and say: 'Both of these matatu drivers leave Kencom Bus Stop at exactly the same time. Both drive exactly 8 km. But one arrives at Westlands, the other at South B. I thought the same distance means the same place.' Pause for 10 seconds, then say: 'Open your exercise books. Write the date and the heading: PREDICTION. What information is missing from the label 8 km that would explain how two journeys of the same distance reach completely different places?' INDIVIDUAL WRITE (2 min): Circulate silently. Do not answer questions or affirm any prediction. Note learners who write 'direction' — they will be useful for discussion. THINK-PAIR (1 min): Say 'Share your prediction with your partner. Do not change your own writing — just listen and compare.' COLD-CALL SHARE (2 min): Cold-call exactly 2 pairs. After each response, write the key word from their prediction on the board with no judgment. Use: 'Interesting. What made you think that?'

records.value: The teacher formally introduces the terms VECTOR and SCALAR with definitions, and learners immediately apply the definitions to classify a set of eight Kenyan-context quantities. DEFINITION PHASE (4 min): The teacher writes two definitions on the board and learners copy them into their books: 'A SCALAR quantity is described completely by its magnitude (size) only.' 'A VECTOR quantity is described completely only when both its magnitude AND direction are stated.' The teacher gives one Nairobi-context worked example for each. CLASSIFICATION ACTIVITY (5 min): Learners receive or copy a table of eight quantities: (1) Temperature in Nairobi today: 22°C; (2) Wind speed at Kisumu Airport: 15 km/h blowing from Lake Victoria towards the east; (3) Mass of a 90 kg bag of maize at Wakulima Market; (4) Displacement of the Likoni Ferry from Mombasa mainland to Mombasa Island; (5) Distance run by Eliud Kipchoge in a training session: 32 km; (6) Force applied by a porter pushing a mkokoteni (handcart) northward along River Road; (7) Time taken to cook ugali: 20 minutes; (8) Velocity of a bodaboda travelling at 40 km/h heading south on Ngong Road. Learners classify each as Vector or Scalar and write a short reason for each. They work individually for 4 minutes, then compare with a partner for 1 minute. WHOLE-CLASS DEBRIEF (4 min): the class discusses the four richest items (2, 4, 6 and 8).

records.value: DEFINITION INTRODUCTION (4 min): Write SCALAR and VECTOR as large headings on the board. Say: 'We now have a name for the two things a journey needs.' Write both definitions. Then say: 'Back to our map. Is 8 km a scalar or a vector?' Wait 10 seconds. Cold-call one learner. 'Correct — 8 km is a SCALAR. It has size only. Now what about: 8 km northwest from Kencom towards Westlands — scalar or vector?' Cold-call a different learner. 'Correct — that is a VECTOR. It has both size AND direction. That is why the two matatus ended up in different places — Route A was a vector pointing northwest, Route B a vector pointing southeast. The 8 km label only told us half the story.' CLASSIFICATION ACTIVITY (5 min): Distribute or display the table of eight quantities. Say: 'Work alone. For each quantity, write V for vector or S for scalar, and write a short reason — magnitude only OR magnitude plus direction.' Set a 4-minute individual timer, then: 'Compare with your partner for one minute. Circle any one you disagree on.' WHOLE-CLASS DEBRIEF (4 min): Cold-call learners for items 2, 4, 6 and 8, the four most pedagogically rich items. For each, ask: 'Which did you choose and WHY?' Use disagreements as teachable moments. LANGUAGE SUPPORT: write the key words on the wall with a picture or arrow beside each: distance (umbali), direction (mwelekeo), size/magnitude (ukubwa), arrow (mshale), vector (vekta). Let learners discuss in Kiswahili or their mother tongue first, then say the sentence in English using the frame 'A scalar has ___ only; a vector has ___ and ___.' ACCESS: learners who find drawing or reading small print difficult can show a vector by walking it on a floor grid or by laying string on the desk map. Key debrief points: Item 2 (wind speed 15 km/h blowing east) — VECTOR because direction is stated; contrast with 'wind speed 15 km/h' alone which would be scalar. Item 4 (Likoni Ferry displacement) — VECTOR because it specifies mainland to island, a clear direction. Item 7 (time 20 minutes) — SCALAR, time has no direction.

records.value: DQB SETUP (before this phase): Prepare a dedicated corner of the classroom wall or a section of the whiteboard labelled 'OUR DRIVING QUESTION BOARD — VECTORS.' Write at the top in large print: 'WHY do two matatu journeys of exactly the same distance from Nairobi's CBD end up at completely different destinations — and what mathematical tool do we need to describe a journey completely?' Below this, draw three columns with headers (A), (B), (C) as described. INDIVIDUAL QUESTION WRITING (2 min): Distribute sticky notes or small paper slips. Say: 'What questions are still in your head about vectors? Write ONE question. Do not worry if it sounds basic. Every question goes up.' POSTING (2 min): Invite learners to come up in rows and post their questions under the column that fits best; the teacher helps if unsure. READ-ALOUD AND STAR ANNOTATION (1 min): Read 3–4 questions aloud, one or two from each column, and place a star (★) next to 2–3 questions that align with upcoming lessons (e.g., 'How do you add two vectors together?', 'Can you show vectors on a graph?'). Learners label their arrows with: (a) the distance (8 km) and (b) their best attempt at a direction (e.g., 'NW' or 'towards Westlands'). Learners keep this initial model — it will be revised in every subsequent lesson as new vector concepts are learned.

records.value: INITIAL MODEL INTRODUCTION (1 min): Say: 'In mathematics, a model is a way of representing a situation so we can analyse it. Every lesson in this unit, you will update your model of the matatu journey. Today you make your FIRST model — rough and incomplete, and that is completely fine.' Distribute the 4×4 grid template (or ask learners to draw a simple grid). Say: 'Mark Kencom at the centre. Draw Route A going northwest to Westlands with an arrow and Route B going southeast to South B with an arrow. Label each arrow with 8 km and the direction as best you can.' Give 2 minutes. CLAIM-EVIDENCE-REASONING FRAME (2 min): Write the CER frame on the board. Say: 'Below your diagram, complete these three sentences, using the map, the demonstration and today's definitions as evidence.' Circulate. Prompt any learner who writes 'distance alone is enough': 'Look at your two arrows — do they go to the same place? So is distance alone enough?' Cold-call 1 learner to read their CER aloud. CLOSE THE LESSON (1 min): Say: 'Keep this model safe — it is the beginning of something. Today the most important thing you leave with is this: 8 km is only half the story. A matatu journey is a vector — it needs direction AND distance.'

records.value: Learners work in pairs with a printed A4 squared-paper grid on which vector **a** (Kencom → University of Nairobi) and vector **b** (University of Nairobi → GPO) are already plotted as directed line segments. The grid has a scale: 1 square = 100 m. The activity has two parts completed in sequence. PART A — Triangle Law (tip-to-tail), 5 minutes: Learners (i) confirm that vector **b** already starts at the tip of vector **a** (tip-to-tail arrangement), (ii) draw the resultant vector **r = a + b** as the arrow from the tail of **a** to the tip of **b**, (iii) use a ruler to measure its length in grid squares. PART B — Column Vector Addition, 4 minutes: Learners read off the column vectors for **a** and **b** from the grid (counting squares right/up for positive, left/down for negative), then add them algebraically: if **a** = (3, 4) and **b** = (5, −2) then **a + b** = (8, 2). They verify that the column vector (8, 2) matches the drawn resultant arrow. The parallelogram law is then shown by the teacher on a class poster/slide (2 minutes): both vectors are redrawn from the same starting point (tail-to-tail) and the resultant is the diagonal of the completed parallelogram. Learners compare it with their own result and do not draw it themselves.

records.value: Learners receive a printed or copied Activity Sheet containing a Nairobi-style 1 cm grid with vector d already drawn as 2 units East and 1 unit North (column vector: d = (2, 1)ᵀ). Task instructions guide them through four constructions in pairs (6 minutes): (A) Draw 3d — start from the same origin, count 3 × 2 = 6 units East and 3 × 1 = 3 units North. Label it. (B) Draw ½d — count 1 unit East and ½ unit North. Label it. (C) Draw −d — count 2 units West and 1 unit South. Label it. (D) Draw −2d — count 4 units West and 2 units South. Label it. After drawing, each pair completes an observation table (3 minutes): for each vector, record (i) the column vector form, (ii) the magnitude (using Pythagoras), (iii) same direction as d / opposite / neither, (iv) same line of action as d: yes/no. Learners then write one sentence (2 minutes) summarising what scalar multiplication does to a vector's direction, and say which destination on the Nairobi grid Kamau would reach in each case.

1. Distribute activity sheets. Say: 'You have 11 minutes for this whole phase: four constructions, the table and one summary sentence. Use a ruler. Each square on the grid represents 1 km on the Nairobi map.' (For the magnitude column, learners use Pythagoras' theorem on the right-angled triangle formed by the two components, which they know from Junior School; Lesson 6 turns this into the formula |v| = √(x² + y²).)

records.value: The teacher facilitates a whole-class discussion to formalise findings from the Observe phase (3 minutes). Learners contribute the pattern statements they wrote, and the teacher scribes a class definition on the board: 'If k is a scalar and a is a vector, then ka is a vector with magnitude |k|×|a|, same line of action as a, direction preserved if k > 0, and direction reversed if k < 0.' Learners then work individually on one application problem set in a Kenyan context (4 minutes): Akinyi the matatu tout records that her matatu covers vector r = (3, −4)ᵀ km from Kisumu Bus Park to the fish market at Dunga Beach. Write in column form: 2r, −r, ½r. Calculate the magnitude of each. (The maize delivery truck problem — if −m takes the truck back to Eldoret, sketch m, −m and 3m — is an extension for early finishers or homework.) Finally, the teacher introduces vector subtraction (5 minutes): 'a − b means a + (−b). To go from Westlands back to Kencom and then on to South B, we add the reverse of the first journey to the second.' Learners practise: given a = (5, 2)ᵀ and b = (3, 6)ᵀ, find a − b algebraically and check it geometrically on the grid.

records.value: Time budget for the 40-minute period: Predict 5, Observe 9, Explain 14, Driving Question Board 4, Model Building 7, transitions 1. Lesson 5 is the primary EXPLAIN lesson in the 8-lesson vectors sequence. Learners move from geometric arrow representations (Lessons 1–4) to algebraic column vector notation. Using a simplified Cartesian grid of central Nairobi — where O = Kencom Bus Stop (origin), A = Kenyatta International Conference Centre (KICC), and B = Uhuru Park — learners plot position vectors OA⃗ and OB⃗, write them as column vectors, and derive the displacement vector AB⃗ = OB⃗ − OA⃗. The lesson resolves the core puzzle of the anchoring phenomenon: the two matatu drivers' journeys can now be written as distinct column vectors with the same magnitude but different components, proving that distance (scalar) alone cannot distinguish them — only the full column vector can. Learners update the Driving Question Board and revise their cumulative vector model of Nairobi. Core competencies developed include Learning to Learn and Self-Efficacy, with values of Responsibility and Unity embedded throughout.

records.value: Time budget for the 40-minute period: Predict 5, Observe 9, Explain 14, Driving Question Board 4, Model Building 7, transitions 1. Learners begin by predicting how a one-way road arrow on a Nairobi street map could be expressed as a column vector. They then observe a worked demonstration of translating a triangle on a Cartesian plane using a given translation vector, noticing that every vertex shifts by exactly the same vector. In the Explain phase, pairs perform their own translations and reverse-engineer translation vectors from object–image pairs, connecting each result back to the matatu phenomenon. The Driving Question Board is updated with new consensus statements and remaining questions. Finally, learners revise their cumulative geometric model to incorporate translation vectors alongside earlier transformation diagrams. The road-safety context — directional arrows as translation instructions — runs throughout.

records.value: At the board, say: 'I am going to move triangle KNB. Every single vertex — K, N, and B — will be shifted by the same translation vector t equals, column vector, 4 on top, 2 on the bottom. Watch what happens to K first.' Plot K(1,1), draw the vector arrow 4 right and 2 up, mark K'(5,3). Say: 'K moved 4 right and 2 up. Now N.' Repeat for N and B. Draw the full image triangle with a dashed outline. Say: 'What do you notice about the three arrows I drew?' WAIT 10 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner. Expect: 'They are all the same.' Confirm: 'Exactly — every point moved by the identical vector. That is the definition of a translation.' (5 minutes so far.) Then reveal the quadrilateral MJUA with its pre-drawn image. Say: 'Work out the translation vector from each vertex to its image. If a learner reads a wrong sign (e.g., negative instead of positive), say: 'Check your direction — which way did the x-component move? Left means negative.' Do not move on until consensus is reached that all four vectors are identical.

Three road arrows are drawn at different points, all pointing in the same direction. Learners express each arrow as a translation vector in column form and explain in one sentence what it means that all three arrows are equal vectors, and say what a road arrow does NOT tell a driver (how far to go). records.value: In this 40-minute capstone lesson (time budget: Predict 4, Observe 6, Explain 15, Final DQB Answer 7, Model Building 7, transitions 1), learners work in groups of four to solve a structured multi-leg vector journey problem set on a simplified sketch map of Nakuru town (landmarks include Nakuru CBD matatu terminus, Westside Mall, Nakuru National Park gate, Lake Nakuru viewpoint, and the Agricultural Society of Kenya [ASK] Showground). Each group receives the map, a task card, and a grid overlay. They describe each leg as a column vector, sum the vectors to find the resultant displacement, compute its magnitude, find the midpoint of the journey, and state the translation vector from start to finish. Groups then compare posters in a short gallery walk. The lesson closes with a Final DQB Review in which every learner independently writes a full answer to the driving question, explicitly comparing their Day-1 thinking with their current understanding. The teacher facilitates a whole-class share-out of the final explanation and celebrates the intellectual journey the class has made from scalar distance to vectors.

records.value: Each group now works through the five mathematical tasks on their Task Card, recording all working on a large sheet of manila paper (for gallery display; 11 minutes): Task 1 — Write each leg as a column vector. Task 2 — Add the three column vectors to find the resultant displacement vector. Task 3 — Find the magnitude of the resultant displacement vector (to 2 decimal places). Task 4 — Given that the start point (Nakuru CBD Terminus) has position vector (2; 1) relative to a fixed origin O at the bottom-left of the grid, find the position vector of the endpoint and hence determine the midpoint of the journey (start to finish). Task 5 — State the translation vector that maps the start point to the endpoint and explain in one sentence what this vector tells a matatu driver. After completing calculations, each group writes a one-sentence 'Vector Story' summarising the journey using correct mathematical language. records.value: The two matatus end up in different places because the distance '8 km' is a scalar. It gives only the magnitude of the journey and says nothing about direction. Both drivers are labelled with the same distance from Kencom, but their directions differ, so their displacement vectors differ. In Part 2, w = (−6; 5) and s = (5; −6) both have a magnitude of about 7.8 km. This is roughly 8 km on our simplified grid, so the two journeys really do have the same size; what separates them is that their components differ, so they point in clearly different directions (north-west and south-east) and the endpoints are Westlands and South B. The tool we need is the vector, which carries both magnitude and direction and can be written as an arrow or as a column vector. For the Nakuru journey, I would write each leg (CBD Terminus to Westside Mall, Westside Mall to the ASK Showground, ASK Showground to the Lake Nakuru Viewpoint) as a column vector. I would add the three column vectors component by component to get the resultant displacement from the start to the finish. I would find its magnitude with Pythagoras' theorem, √(x² + y²). With the legs (3; 4), (5; −2) and (−2; 6) the resultant is (6; 8) and its magnitude is √(36 + 64) = 10 km. The total distance travelled is the sum of the lengths of all three legs, 5 + √29 + √40 ≈ 16.7 km, but the displacement is the single straight-line vector from start to finish, so the two are not equal here (16.7 km against 10 km): they would be equal only if every leg pointed the same way. The translation vector from the start to the finish is the same as this resultant. On Day 1 I thought that travelling the same distance should bring you to the same place. Now I understand that distance is a scalar, and that direction as well as size is needed to describe a journey completely and to predict where it ends.
